I’m extremely disappointed with my experience at Petfolk.

I brought my dog in for a recurring skin irritation that happens around the same time each year. This is the second time I’ve been told the exact same thing by Petfolk. Last year, when the area became infected, they also insisted it was caused by fleas, yet my dog has never had a single flea in his life.

His father has severe grass allergies, so I asked the vet to consider environmental allergies as a possible cause. My dog is an indoor dog, gets professionally groomed every month, doesn’t go to dog parks or interact with other dogs, and has never had fleas.

The vet Megan immediately insisted it was fleas. She searched through his coat, said she saw flea eggs (it was dirt), then admitted she couldn’t actually find any fleas. A moment later she claimed she had found one, but when I leaned in to look, she said it had “jumped away.” Every time I tried to explain my concerns or my dog’s history, I felt dismissed instead of listened to.

The most frustrating part was wasting my time and leaving without real answers. I wasn’t asking the vet to agree with me—I was asking her to consider allergies and investigate other possibilities instead of insisting on one explanation before discussing anything else.

To me, the entire visit felt like it was more about selling an overpriced flea preventative (cheaper on chewy) than finding the actual cause of my dog’s recurring skin irritation. I left feeling talked down to, out $500, and with the same unresolved issue I came in with. I will not be returning.

I rarely leave negative reviews, but after giving Petfolk multiple chances, I feel it’s important to share my experience.

I enrolled both my dog, Violet, and my cat, Dinah, because I originally loved Petfolk’s low-stress approach. We were greeted immediately, given lavender calming blankets, and taken straight to an exam room. That level of care was a big reason I chose Petfolk.

Unfortunately, my experiences steadily declined. Violet had a medical issue that required multiple visits without being resolved. I eventually sought a second opinion elsewhere, where the issue was identified and treated right away.

At Violet’s annual visit, we arrived on time for a 4 PM appointment but waited about 15 minutes before anyone acknowledged us and then nearly another 40 minutes in an exam room without seeing a veterinarian. There was little communication, and after almost an hour without receiving care, I asked to cancel the appointment and left.

What concerned me most, however, came afterward when I reviewed my pets’ medical records. I found vaccines and other services documented as having been given that I know did not occur, including rabies and Bordetella vaccines. The records contained specific details such as injection sites, manufacturer/lot information, and prescription numbers. Dinah’s my cats records also contained a vaccine documented as given when she was not even at the clinic.

I brought these discrepancies to Petfolk and was told they were “human error.” Even after the records were resubmitted, I still found inaccuracies. My account was also subsequently deleted/disappeared.

This is much more than a paperwork issue. Inaccurate vaccine records can affect future veterinary care and can cause serious problems with boarding, grooming, daycare, and other facilities that rely on vaccination records.

Because of the seriousness of the discrepancies, I reported the issue to the appropriate regulatory board. I’m sharing this so current and future Petfolk clients know to carefully review their pets’ records and make sure everything documented actually happened.

I truly hope Petfolk can return to the level of care and compassion that originally made them stand out, but unfortunately, I no longer feel comfortable entrusting them with Violet or Dinah’s care.

Dr Allstott examined him Sunday morning and said  he had a severe herniation  which required immediate surgery.  She said there were two neurologist in San Antonio  that could do surgery on Monday.  But   College Station, small animal Hospital could do  surgery same day on Sunday.

We told  Dr Allstott we’d take AP to College station Sunday. When we arrived at the hospital at 2:30pm there was no neurologist or anesthesiologist working. We were told we’d have to wait till Monday. On Monday his condition was worse.  The MRI and surgery weren’t done until 06:00pm.  He developed  myelomalacia due to the delay in treatment and died Thursday.
